newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICAN ENERGY WHITE PAPER SHAPING UP.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICAN ENERGY WHITE PAPER SHAPING UP.

text.p: The long-awaited energy policy white paper could be finalised this year, Minerals and Energy Department chief director of energy Johann Basson said on Wednesday.

Although this is further away from finalisation than many in the oil industry would like, Basson also outlined some of the factors that would have to be taken into consideration in any new energy policy.
Briefing the National Council of Provinces economic and foreign affairs committee, Basson said the draft white paper on energy policy "is just about complete in internal form".
"We hope to hand this to the Minister by the end of the month. Whether he will be happy with it as it is...and whether there are changes, I am not sure."
But he hoped that the white paper would be finalised this year and passed through parliament.
He outlined some of the problems that had been experienced in finalising new policies on energy.
"We had a system in the past when security was a primary consideration and this led to a problem in terms of collecting the right data," he said.
"And the data that we have is inadequate for many of the analyses that are required."
Another problem was that the energy sector was institutionally stronger than the department.

Following criticism last year by the International Energy Agency about the weakness in the department's energy policies, Basson said the chief directorate on energy had been upgraded to a branch but it was severely lacked skilled people.
"There is intense debate taking place in the energy sector in terms of policy," Basson said.
"Much of this is contentious. Many of the stakeholders have totally diverse opinions."
Whatever changes were made would, however, have to take into consideration changes that were taking place globally in the energy sector.
"In South Africa we are mainly using coal to a great extent while in other countries there is diversification towards gas, renewable forms of energy, nuclear energy and others," he said.
Another factor was the role of the market and competition.

"It was accepted about 10 years ago that energy is a commodity, nothing different to any commodity that we trade and buy and sell and that you can compete, although many of those are in the form of monpolies.
"And this is something that we will have to give attention to in South Africa because we have limited competition in the energy sector."
It was also a sector where there was a steady movement into the private sector, Basson said.

"If you look at developing countries, many of the large energy institutions belong to the state. The same applies in South Africa, but in developed countries this is all in the private sector and competition takes place freely."

There was also a move towards developing a sector that was sustainable while taking environmental factors into consideration, ensuring the efficient use and production of energy, the use of renewable energy and increased research and development.
